description: Define your Model Context Protocol servers once and generate correct config for Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and VS Code, with import, transfer, and merge.

readme.content:
# mcp-config-sync Keep one canonical MCP server config and generate the client-specific files from it. Write your servers down once, then produce a correct config for Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and any other client that reads an `mcpServers` file, without copying JSON between tools by hand. It also works the other way: import an existing client file back into the canonical shape, move a setup straight from one client to another, and merge a shared config with your own. ![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue) ![Python 3.9+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.9%2B-blue) ![Runtime dependencies: none](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime%20dependencies-none-brightgreen) ## Why I built this I ran the same handful of MCP servers in more than one tool. Every client wants a slightly different file, in a slightly different place, with a slightly different shape, so each time I added a server or rotated a token I edited two or three JSON files and usually got one of them wrong. The shapes are close enough to look the same and different enough to break: - The top-level key is `mcpServers` in Claude Desktop, Cursor, and Windsurf, but `servers` in VS Code and `context_servers` in Zed. - A remote server's address is `url` in most clients but `serverUrl` in Windsurf. - VS Code labels every server with an explicit `type`; Claude Desktop has no `type` field at all; Zed needs `"source": "custom"` or it silently ignores the entry. - Some clients run remote servers, some run local processes only. A field one client respects (`cwd`) is dropped by another. So a value copied from one file into another is often subtly wrong, and the tool just ignores the broken entry. I wanted a single source of truth I could validate once and project out to every client, with a loud warning whenever a target cannot represent something rather than a silent drop. That is all this does, and it tries to do it well: clear errors, no surprises, and no secrets in places they should not be. ## How it works You keep one canonical document (`config.json`). It lists every MCP server you run. Every client file is generated from it, and every converter works in both directions: `sync` writes left to right, `import` reads right to left. ```mermaid flowchart LR canonical["config.json
the canonical config
(the only file you edit)"] canonical <--> cd["Claude Desktop
claude_desktop_config.json"] canonical <--> vs["VS Code
.vscode/mcp.json"] canonical <--> cu["Cursor
.cursor/mcp.json"] canonical <--> ws["Windsurf
~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json"] canonical <--> zd["Zed
settings.json (context_servers)"] canonical <--> gn["generic
mcpServers.json"] ``` Two more operations build on the same converters, so you are never stuck retyping a setup you already have. `transfer` moves a setup from one client to another through the canonical shape, refusing to write anything if the middle step does not validate. `merge` combines several canonical sources into one. ```mermaid flowchart LR src["a file you already have
(say .cursor/mcp.json)"] -->|transfer| mid["canonical shape
validated in memory"] -->|transfer| dst["another client's file
(say Zed settings.json)"] team["team.json"] -->|merge| out["config.json"] personal["personal.json"] -->|merge| out ``` The canonical document is the only file you edit. The generated files are disposable: delete them and run `sync` again. ## Supported clients | Client | File | Top-level key | Remote field | Runs remote servers | Keeps `cwd` | | -------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------ | ------------------- | ----------- | | Claude Desktop | `claude_desktop_config.json` | `mcpServers` | none | no | no | | VS Code | `mcp.json` | `servers` | `url` | yes (http, sse) | yes | | Cursor | `mcp.json` | `mcpServers` | `url` | yes (http, sse) | no | | Windsurf | `mcp_config.json` | `mcpServers` | `serverUrl` | yes (http, sse) | no | | Zed | `settings.json` | `context_servers` | none | no | no | | Generic | `mcpServers.json` | `mcpServers` | `url` | yes (http, sse) | yes | Every column in that table is a place a hand-copied value goes wrong. The generic target keeps every field, including the transport `type` and `cwd`, so it round-trips through this tool without loss and is a safe thing to hand to a client not listed above. ## Why this beats editing each file by hand - **Validate once.** A typo, an unknown field, a remote server with no URL, or a `type` that is not one of `stdio`, `http`, `sse` is reported with the exact path to the problem (for example `servers.filesystem.command`) before any client file is written. - **No silent drops.** When a target cannot represent a server (Claude Desktop and Zed run local servers only) or a field (Cursor and Windsurf have no working directory), it is skipped or dropped with a warning that names what was lost, instead of vanishing quietly the way a hand edit does. - **One place for tokens.** Your tokens live in the single canonical file, not scattered across four client files you then have to keep in sync and remember to keep private. - **Adopt and move setups.** `import` pulls an existing client file into the canonical shape, and `transfer` moves a setup from one client to another in a single step. Switching editors does not mean retyping your servers. - **Combine sources.** `merge` turns a shared team config plus your personal one into a single canonical file, and stops you if both define the same server name with different values. ## The canonical config A canonical document has a `version` and a map of named `servers`. A server is either local (`stdio`) or remote (`http` or `sse`). ```json { "version": "1", "servers": { "filesystem": { "type": "stdio", "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."], "env": { "LOG_LEVEL": "info" } }, "company-api": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/v1", "headers": { "Authorization": "[REDACTED-BEARER_TOKEN]" } } } } ``` Fields: - `version` (required): schema version, currently `"1"`. - `servers` (required): map of server name to definition. Names match `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`. - `type` (required): `stdio`, `http`, or `sse`. - For `stdio`: `command` (required), plus optional `args`, `env`, `cwd`. - For `http` and `sse`: `url` (required), plus optional `headers`. See `config.example.json` for a fuller starting point. ## Install ```bash git clone https://github.com/EdgeF-4/mcp-config-sync.git cd mcp-config-sync pip install -e . ``` That installs the `mcp-config-sync` command. If you would rather not install, run it as a module from the repo root with `python -m mcp_config_sync ...`. There are no runtime dependencies; it is the standard library only. ## Quick start ```bash cp config.example.json config.json chmod 600 config.json # the canonical file holds your tokens # edit config.json: add your servers and real tokens mcp-config-sync validate # check the file mcp-config-sync convert --client vscode # print one client's config mcp-config-sync sync --out-dir dist # write every client's config ``` ## Run it with Docker If you would rather not install anything, build the image once and run the tool against whatever directory you mount: ```bash docker build -t mcp-config-sync . docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" mcp-config-sync validate docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" mcp-config-sync sync --out-dir dist docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" mcp-config-sync list-clients ``` The image holds the tool and nothing else. Your `config.json` stays on your machine and is read through the mount, so tokens are never baked into a layer (`.dockerignore` keeps it out of the build context too). On Linux, add `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` so the files `sync` writes are owned by you rather than root. ## Commands All commands that read the canonical file take `--config` (default `config.json`). ### validate Read the canonical config and report every problem it finds at once, each with a dotted path to the exact spot. ```bash mcp-config-sync validate mcp-config-sync validate --config config.json ``` ``` config.json is not valid: servers.filesystem.command: missing required field for a stdio server servers.company-api.url: must start with http:// or https:// ``` ### convert Generate one client's config. Prints to standard output, or writes a file with `--out`. Anything the client cannot represent is reported as a warning. ```bash mcp-config-sync convert --client claude-desktop mcp-config-sync convert --client vscode --out .vscode/mcp.json ``` ### sync Write every client's config under `--out-dir` (default `dist`), one folder per client. Pass `--client` one or more times to limit which ones. ```bash mcp-config-sync sync --out-dir dist mcp-config-sync sync --client cursor --client zed --out-dir dist ``` ``` wrote dist/claude-desktop/claude_desktop_config.json wrote dist/cursor/mcp.json wrote dist/generic/mcpServers.json wrote dist/vscode/mcp.json wrote dist/windsurf/mcp_config.json wrote dist/zed/settings.json ``` ### import Read a client's own file back into the canonical shape, so you can adopt a setup you already have instead of retyping it. Prints the canonical config, or writes it with `--out`. ```bash mcp-config-sync import --client cursor --in ~/.cursor/mcp.json mcp-config-sync import --client claude-desktop \ --in "~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json" \ --out config.json ``` When a source file does not state a remote server's transport, `http` is assumed and a warning says so, so you can correct it if it should be `sse`. ### transfer Move a setup straight from one client's file to another, through the canonical shape, in a single step. Warnings from both the import and the export are shown together. ```bash mcp-config-sync transfer --from cursor --to zed --in ~/.cursor/mcp.json mcp-config-sync transfer --from claude-desktop --to vscode \ --in claude_desktop_config.json --out .vscode/mcp.json ``` ### merge Combine several canonical configs into one, in the order given. This is how a shared team config and your personal one become a single source of truth. If two sources name the same server, the default is to stop and list the clashes; pass `--on-conflict first` or `--on-conflict last` to pick a winner. ```bash mcp-config-sync merge team.json personal.json --out config.json mcp-config-sync merge base.json overrides.json --on-conflict last ``` ### list-clients Show the registered clients and where each expects its file. ```bash mcp-config-sync list-clients ``` ## Secrets and file permissions The canonical file doubles as where your tokens live, inside `env` and `headers`. Because of that: - `config.json` is gitignored. Commit `config.example.json` instead, with placeholder values. - Keep it private with `chmod 600 config.json`. The tool warns you whenever it reads a config that other users can read, and reminds you to lock down any canonical file it writes. - Tokens stay in this one file. There is no `.env` and nothing is read from the environment. ## Project layout ``` src/mcp_config_sync/ schema.py the canonical shape, in one place validate.py collects every problem, never raises on bad input canonical.py load the file and check its permissions converters/ one module per client, each works in both directions operations.py transfer (round-trip) and merge registry.py where clients register cli.py validate, convert, sync, import, transfer, merge, list-clients tests/ the test suite config.example.json Dockerfile a containerized copy of the CLI, nothing else inside ``` ## Adding a client Each converter is one small module under `converters/` that subclasses `Converter`: set `client_id`, `display_name`, and `output_filename`, implement `convert` (canonical to client) and `to_canonical` (client back to canonical), then register the class in `registry.py`. The canonical shape and the validator are shared, so a new client cannot drift from the format the rest of the tool agrees on. Shared import inference for `mcpServers`-style files lives in `converters/_helpers.py`. ## Roadmap - Externalize secrets through VS Code `inputs` and Cursor `${env:...}` so the generated files can ship without tokens inlined. - More clients as their config formats stabilize. ## License MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
